text: Your money is only worth what its government can defend.
In 1992, Britain spent billions defending the pound for one day.
Then, it lost.
Why?
September 16, 1992.
By 9am, the Bank of England had already spent more than a billion pounds buying back its own currency.
At 11, it raised interest rates from 10 to 12 percent.
At 215, it promised 15.
In the money markets, overnight cash was quoted at 100 percent.
None of it worked.
By about 7.30 that evening, it was over.
In a few hours, Britain had thrown more than 22 billion dollars at the market.
And lost.
A hundred percent for one night?
Pricier than a hotel in peak season.
On the other side of that trade sat one fund run out of New York, holding a bet of about
ten billion dollars that Britain would break its own promise.
It walked away with about a billion.
So how does one fund beat a whole country?
To answer that, we need to go back to a promise Britain made two years earlier.
Imagine your rupee, your pound, or your dollar changed value against its neighbors every single day.
For a factory selling across Europe in the 1980s, that was normal.
Profits could vanish because a currency wobbled overnight.
So in 1979, a group of European countries built a fence.
It was called the Exchange Rate Mechanism, or ERM. Each currency could drift, but only
inside a band. Hit the edge of the band and the central bank had to step in and defend
it. Britain stayed out for over a decade. Then on October 8, 1990, it jumped in. The
2.95 Deutschmarks. The band, 6% either way. The floor, 2.778. Below that, the Bank of
England had to buy pounds, whatever it cost. The man who signed Britain up was the Finance
Minister, Chancellor John Major. The same day, rates were cut from 15 to 14%. Why tie
yourself to Germany? Because Britain had a problem. In 1990, inflation hit 10.9%. Germany's
Central Bank, the Bundesbank, was the toughest inflation fighter in the world.
Peg your money to the Deutsche Mark and you borrow its reputation.
It's like a student who can't stop spending, handing his card to the

Here's the catch.
Days before Britain joined, East and West Germany reunited.
Rebuilding the East cost enormous sums, and German money started growing too fast.
By July 1992, German money supply was running around 9%, against a target of 3.5 to 5.5.
So the Bundesbank did what it always did. It raised rates.

British inflation was down to 3.6%. The medicine had done its job. But Britain couldn't stop
taking it. Britain needed cheaper money, but with the pound pinned near its floor, it couldn't cut
rates without the pound sinking through it. Its interest rates were now set, in effect,
by a central bank in Frankfurt, worrying about Berlin.
That's the mirage in this story.
A fixed exchange rate looks like a fact.
It isn't.
It's a promise.
And it only holds while someone is willing and able to defend it.
So, the price on me is just a promise?
You keep discovering that.
Across the Atlantic, someone was watching that promise very closely.
George Soros ran the Quantum Fund in New York.
Day to day it was managed by Stanley Druckenmiller, and by most accounts the pound trade was his
idea.
Here's how you bet against a currency.
You borrow pounds and immediately sell them for Deutschmarks at around $2.78.
If the pound later falls to, say, $2.50, you buy those pounds back cheaper, return what
you borrowed, and keep the difference.
Now look at the odds.
The pound was sitting near its floor.
If Britain held the line, the pound could only rise a little, so the bet loses a little.
If Britain broke, the pound could fall a long way, and the bet wins big.
Heads, you lose a little, tails, you win a lot.
Traders dream of a bet like that.
But wait, isn't the Bank of England unbeatable?
It can print as many pounds as it likes.
Here's the problem.
To hold up the pound, it has to buy pounds and pay for them in other currencies, like
Deutsche Marks and dollars.

At 7.30pm, Lamont walks out into the Treasury Courtyard and announces that the pound is suspended

The 15% hike is cancelled that night.
The next morning, rates are back to 10.
In a few hours, Britain had sold more than $22 billion of its reserves trying to hold
a price the market no longer believed.
Freed from its floor, the pound fell.
By the end of 1992, it was around 2.45 Deutschmarks, roughly 17% below the rate Britain had promised.
Against the dollar, it slid from about 1.85 to about 1.52.
Soros and his fund made about a billion dollars,
and a hedge fund manager almost nobody outside finance had heard of got a new name.
The man who broke the Bank of England.
And Britain? Spending reserves isn't the same as losing them.
The real loss came from buying pounds at the old price and watching them fall.
When Treasury papers were finally released in 2005, the best estimate of the cost was 3.3 billion pounds.

Now the twist. Without the peg, Britain could finally set its own rates. By November,
Labour they were down to 7%.
In October 1992, it adopted something new, an inflation target, a public goal of 1-4%.
And on May 6, 1997, just days after winning power, Labour's new Chancellor, Gordon Brown,
gave the Bank of England the power to set rates itself.
Lamont says Brown phoned him the day before to say Labour was taking his advice.

So was Soros the villain? He didn't create Britain's problem. He spotted it. A country
had promised a price it couldn't afford to keep, and he bet that the promise would
break before the bank did.
That's the lesson, and it's bigger than 1992. Whenever someone promises you a fixed price
while the market quietly disagrees, a currency peg, a guaranteed return, a coin that's always
worth one dollar, ask one question. Who's defending it, and how deep are their pockets?
So every promise has a price tag.
And a limit, darling.
A promise is only as strong as what stands behind it.
When that runs out, the mirage disappears.
Money is full of promises like this one.
Prices, pegs, and deals that aren't what they seem.
